Question: Let \(S\) be a square of side length \(1.\) Two points are chosen independently at random on the sides of \(S.\) The probability that the straight-line distance between the points is at least \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) is \(\dfrac{a-b\pi}{c},\) where \(a,\) \(b,\) and \(c\) are positive integers with \(\gcd(a,b,c)=1.\) What is \(a+b+c?\)
Solution:
Use the standard interpretation that each point is chosen uniformly along the perimeter. Because the four sides have equal length, each point is equally likely to lie on any side. Vertices have probability zero, so they may be assigned to either incident side.

Distinguish the first point from the second. There are \(4\cdot4=16\) equally likely ordered pairs of sides. For any fixed pair of sides, describe the two points by their distances \(u\) and \(v\) from chosen endpoints, where \(0\le u,v\le1\). Independence and uniform sampling make \((u,v)\) uniform in a unit square, so the probability within that square equals the favorable area.

If the points are on the same side, measure both coordinates from the same endpoint. Their distance is \(|u-v|\). The condition \(|u-v|\ge\tfrac12\) describes two corner triangles, each with perpendicular legs of length \(\tfrac12\). Their total area is
\[
2\left(\frac12\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12\right)=\frac14.
\]
There are four ordered pairs of this type.

If the sides are adjacent, measure \(u\) and \(v\) from their shared corner. By the Pythagorean theorem, the distance squared is \(u^2+v^2\). Thus the points are too close precisely when
\[
u^2+v^2<\frac14.
\]
Within the parameter square, this is a quarter disk of radius \(\tfrac12\), with area \(\pi/16\). The favorable area is therefore \(1-\pi/16\). Each first side has two adjacent sides, giving eight ordered pairs of this type.

If the sides are opposite, their perpendicular separation is \(1\), so every pair of points has distance at least \(1\). The entire parameter square is favorable. There are four ordered pairs of this type.

These three types exhaust the sixteen ordered side pairs without overlap, apart from the irrelevant vertex cases. The distance-equality boundaries are line segments or circular arcs and have zero area. Hence the required probability, including equality, is
\[
\frac{4(1/4)+8(1-\pi/16)+4}{16}
=\frac{26-\pi}{32}.
\]
Since \(\gcd(26,1,32)=1\), we have \(a=26\), \(b=1\), and \(c=32\). Therefore \(a+b+c=\boxed{59}\), choice A.
